newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German sick pay deal sparks peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German sick pay deal sparks peace hopes.

text.p: A surprise decision by metal and engineering employers in the German state of Lower Saxony not to enforce a law cutting sick pay sparked hopes on Thursday of a wider settlement averting threatened strikes in the sector.

Negotiators said that after 13 hours of talks in the northern town of Hanover they had agreed a package maintaining sick pay at 100 percent of salary, overriding an unpopular new law allowing employers to cut sick pay to 80 percent.
"The accord is a breakthrough in the metal industry," Juergen Peters, chief negotiator for the IG Metall trade union said early on Thursday.
The law had been introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in October as part of austerity measures aimed at securing German entry to European economic and monetary union in 1999.

While Peters stressed that the deal was only applicable to the 90,000 metal and engineering workers in Lower Saxony, union officials said they were now more optimistic that similar agreements could be reached elsewhere in the industry.
"When employers participate as they did in Lower Saxony, there will be deals in other regions -- that is my hope at least," a spokeswoman at IG Metall's headquarters in Frankfurt said.

An IG Metall official in the steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia, where a similar attempt to end the dispute failed last week, said she was now optimistic that a deal could be reached before Christmas.
All-out strikes in the sector, where stoppages have already cost firms such as Daimler Benz AG's car unit Mercedes millions of marks, had been seen as increasingly likely to start next spring.

Employer representatives, while noticeably less enthusiastic about the deal than their union counterparts, said the full package would for the average firm in the sector mean a cost increase of less than one percent next year.
"Regional employer federations will in the next weeks decide whether they want to take on the Hanover agreement," the Gesamtmetall metal and engineering employers group said in a statement.
But Gesamtmetall, which had hoped that cuts to sick pay would be the first of series of other reductions in German labour costs, said "variations were to be expected" on the content of the package.
Under the deal, Lower Saxony workers will receive a wage increase of 1.5 percent from April, 1997 and a further rise of 2.5 percent from April 1, 1998.

In return for full sick pay, end-of-year bonuses will however fall by five percent to 55 percent of salary. Furthermore, overtime bonuses will no longer be taken into account when calculating sick payments.

The deal comes as employers in other sections of German industry have decided to implement the sick pay cuts despite a rising tide of protests from workers in normally peaceable sectors such as the banking industry.
Unions have warned of further protests by bank workers if talks with employers due to start on Monday do not yield an agreement.
Chemical industry employers and union leaders were also meeting on Thursday to discuss a solution in their sector. --Bonn Newsroom +49 228 260 97150
